lesson.title: Thinking About Behavior: Bandura's Social-Cognitive Leap
lesson.summary: Albert Bandura's social-cognitive theory expands social learning theory by showing that cognitive processes, expectations, beliefs, and self-evaluation, actively shape how people learn and act, not just observation and imitation alone.
lesson.body:
Social learning theory already showed that people learn a great deal by watching others: a child sees a peer get praised for sharing and becomes more likely to share too, without ever needing to be reinforced directly. Bandura's own early work, including his well known studies of children imitating aggressive models, established that observation and modeling are powerful teachers. Social-cognitive theory takes that foundation and asks a further question: once we have observed a model, what happens inside the mind that determines whether we actually adopt the behavior?

Bandura's answer was that cognition does most of the work. People do not simply absorb what they see, they interpret it. They form expectations about what a behavior is likely to produce, they judge whether they are capable of performing it themselves, and they set internal standards they use to evaluate their own actions afterward. This was a deliberate departure from strict behaviorism, which tended to treat the person as a passive relay between stimulus and response. Bandura instead described people as active agents who think about, anticipate, and regulate their own behavior rather than simply reacting to whatever reinforcement history has shaped them.

This cognitive layer connects directly to self-concept. As children and adults watch others, succeed or fail at things themselves, and receive feedback, they build an internal picture of who they are and what they are capable of. That self-concept is not a fixed trait handed down at birth, it is constructed and revised through exactly the kind of observation, comparison, and self-evaluation that social-cognitive theory describes. A student who repeatedly watches classmates struggle with a subject she finds easy may come to see herself as strong in that area, and that self-concept then guides how she approaches future challenges in it.

One reason social-cognitive theory improved on a purely observational account of learning is that it explains why some modeled behaviors take hold and others do not. A person is more likely to adopt a behavior they have seen modeled when they expect it to lead to a good outcome, when they believe they are capable of carrying it out successfully, and when the model seems similar enough to themselves that the lesson feels applicable. None of that can be explained by imitation alone, it requires an internal, evaluative process. That internal process, and specifically the person's belief in their own capability, becomes central in the next idea: reciprocal determinism.
